intro: You have probably heard the word Illuminati in a video, a song or a joke. Online it is often used to mean a hidden group that secretly runs the world. Fewer people know that the Illuminati were a real, small society. A law professor founded it in Bavaria, in southern Germany, in 1776. The government banned it within ten years.

This unit follows two stories. The first is the real order: its founder, its code names, its quarrels, the laws against it and the police searches that exposed its papers. The second is the legend that grew after the order ended. Writers blamed it for the French Revolution. Ministers warned Americans about it. In the 1960s and 1970s, joke books and novels, one begun in Chicago, gave it new life.

Along the way you will practice skills historians use every day. You will read primary sources, spot bias and test a claim for corroboration. You will sort claims into documented, disputed and unsupported. By the end, you will be able to explain what the evidence shows about the Illuminati and why the legend lasts.
bigQuestion: How can a real secret society that lasted less than a decade turn into a legend that people still believe more than two hundred years later?

timeline.t: The Rosicrucian Fama is printed in Kassel, describing a hidden brotherhood
Adam Weishaupt founds the Order of the Illuminati at Ingolstadt, Bavaria

A second edict names the Freemasons and the Illuminati
Officers search Zwack's house at Landshut and seize the order's papers

Robison's Proofs of a Conspiracy and Barruel's Memoirs blame secret societies
Jedidiah Morse warns of the Illuminati in a fast-day sermon in Boston

The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn is founded in London

test.q: Where did Adam Weishaupt found the Illuminati in 1776?
test.why: Weishaupt founded the order at Ingolstadt, where he taught canon law.

test.q: Which idea was central to Weishaupt's order?
choices: Reason, and less church control over learning

Weishaupt used the code name Spartacus, after the leader of a revolt against Rome.

test.q: What role did Baron Adolph Knigge play?
choices: He ordered the house search at Landshut
He wrote the Memoirs of Jacobinism
He helped the order grow through Masonic lodges, then quit in 1784
test.why: Knigge joined in 1780, recruited through lodges and left on 1 July 1784 after quarrels.

choices: Made the Illuminati the official church
Banned secret societies, and then named the Illuminati
Gave Weishaupt a new university post

They come only from the lightning story

That officers searched Zwack's house in 1786
That Bavaria issued edicts in 1784 and 1785
That the government printed the papers in 1787
test.why: The 1787 books credit the house search, not papers found on Lanz.

test.q: Why was John Robison's book taken seriously in 1797?
choices: He had been a leader of the Illuminati
He was a respected Edinburgh scientist
He was the President of the United States
He had found the Rosicrucian tomb
test.why: Robison taught natural philosophy at Edinburgh, so readers trusted him, even though his history was weak.

test.q: Which statement about Barruel and the French Revolution is most accurate?
choices: He proved the Illuminati ran France
He was a member of the Illuminati
He wrote after the Revolution to praise it
He blamed the Revolution on a long plot, quoting real papers that did not prove it
test.why: Barruel quoted the Bavarian papers, but they did not show the order directing events in France.

test.q: Why do historians call the 1798 scare partly partisan?
choices: Many warning ministers were Federalists using it against Jefferson's party
test.why: Historians from Stauffer on note that Federalist clergy used the scare against the Democratic-Republicans.

test.q: How did Washington answer G. W. Snyder in 1798?
choices: He said he had never heard of Freemasonry
He agreed the ideas had spread but did not believe the lodges were spreading them
test.why: Washington drew a distinction between ideas spreading and the lodges, as bodies, spreading them.

test.q: What does the pair of Morse's sermon and Jefferson's 1800 letter show?
choices: That the same evidence can lead to opposite conclusions
That Barruel's book was never read in America
That the Illuminati moved to Boston
test.why: Both drew on the same kind of evidence, yet Morse saw a plot and Jefferson saw a reformer.

test.q: Which fact about the dollar-bill eye is documented?

It was proposed for the Great Seal in 1776 and adopted in 1782

test.q: What made the Golden Dawn different from the Rosicrucian brotherhood of the manifestos?

The Golden Dawn was founded in 1614
The Golden Dawn was banned in Bavaria
The Golden Dawn had no members
test.why: Records show the Golden Dawn's founders, temples and members, while no records show a Rosicrucian brotherhood.

test.q: Which claim about the Illuminati is unsupported?
choices: Bavaria printed its seized papers in 1787
The order survives today and controls world events
test.why: No documentary evidence shows the order continued after the 1780s, so the claim is unsupported.

Separate what a source shows from what a writer claimed it showed.
Give the other side fairly before you answer it.
Use unit terms such as propaganda, corroboration and claims ledger.
End with one sentence that answers the question plainly.

title: The Real Illuminati and the Legend After

chapters.title: Weishaupt's Order, 1776–1785
chapters.bigQuestion: What do the Illuminati's own seized papers show about what the order was, and what it was not?

story.title: A House Search in Landshut
story.kicker: In October 1786, Bavarian officers search a man's home and carry off the papers of a secret order.
paragraphs: It is October 1786, in Landshut, a town in Bavaria in southern Germany. Officers of the Elector, the ruler of Bavaria, arrive at the house of Franz Xaver von Zwack. Zwack had worked for the government as a councillor. Now the government suspects him of something. It believes he is a leader in a banned secret society.

The search lasts two days, the 11th and 12th of October. The officers go through desks, boxes and shelves. They find bundles of letters. They find rule books and lists of members who used strange names from ancient Greece and Rome. They find plans for how the group should grow. Everything is packed up and taken away.

The papers belong to the Order of the Illuminati. The name means the enlightened ones. A law professor named Adam Weishaupt had started it ten years earlier. For most of those years, only members knew its rules. Bavaria had already banned the order in 1784 and 1785. The search was meant to show the public what it had really been.

Then the government did something new. In 1787 it printed the seized papers as a book, by order of the Elector. Anyone could buy it and read the secret order's letters. Today, historians still read those printed papers. They are the best evidence we have about what the real Illuminati wanted and did.
story.think: The government printed a secret group's private papers to turn people against it. Is the enemy's printing of a group's papers good evidence about that group? What would you check?

lessons.title: Ingolstadt, May 1776
lessons.mainIdea: Adam Weishaupt, a young professor of canon law at the University of Ingolstadt in Bavaria, founded the Order of the Illuminati on 1 May 1776.
reading: Ingolstadt is a town on the Danube River in Bavaria. In the 1770s it had Bavaria's main university. One of its teachers was Adam Weishaupt, born in 1748. He taught *canon law*, the law of the Catholic Church. He was still in his twenties, young for a professor.

On 1 May 1776, Weishaupt met with a few of his students to start a club. It was a *secret society*, a group that keeps its membership, rules or meetings hidden from outsiders. He called it the Order of the Illuminati. The name comes from a Latin word for people who have been given light, or understanding.

The date is a favorite of later rumors. 1776 is also the year of the American Declaration of Independence. But no document links the two events. Historians call it a coincidence of the calendar. The date itself comes from the order's own papers, which the Bavarian government later seized and printed.

At the start the order was tiny. Its first members were students and young men at the start of their careers. Weishaupt planned to train them in his ideas and then help them into good jobs. He hoped that over time they would spread those ideas through Bavarian society.

words.d: the body of law made by the Catholic Church for its own members and affairs
a group that keeps its members, rules or meetings hidden from outsiders
two things happening at the same time by chance, with no cause linking them

check.q: Where was Adam Weishaupt teaching when he founded the Illuminati?
choices: The University of Ingolstadt in Bavaria
The University of Edinburgh in Scotland
check.why: The reading says Weishaupt taught canon law at the university in Ingolstadt, Bavaria.

check.q: What subject did Weishaupt teach?
choices: Canon law, the law of the Catholic Church
check.why: Canon law is the law of the Catholic Church, and the reading names it as Weishaupt's subject.

check.q: Why do historians call the link between 1 May 1776 and American independence a coincidence?
choices: Because Weishaupt wrote to Thomas Jefferson that year
Because the order met in Philadelphia

Because the Declaration mentions the Illuminati

lessons.title: Reason Against Control
lessons.mainIdea: Weishaupt's order grew from Enlightenment ideas: trust in reason, and opposition to church control over what students could learn.
reading: The 1700s in Europe are often called the age of the *Enlightenment*. Writers argued that people should use reason and evidence to understand the world. They questioned old authorities, including kings and church leaders. Many Enlightenment thinkers wanted schools, science and books to be freer.

For about two hundred years, members of the Jesuit order, a Catholic order of priests, had shaped teaching at Ingolstadt. In 1773 the pope dissolved the Jesuit order. Weishaupt had been educated at a Jesuit school himself. Yet he was never a Jesuit, and he opposed their influence at his university.

Weishaupt disliked *censorship*, the control of what people are allowed to read, write or say. In Bavaria, church and state officials decided which books were allowed. Weishaupt wanted his students to read freely and think for themselves. He also wanted them to become better people, not just better scholars.

So why keep the order secret? Weishaupt believed open talk of these ideas could cost members their jobs. Critics saw it differently. To them, a hidden group that wanted to place its members in power looked like a plot. Both views appear in writing from the time, and students today can weigh them.

words.d: a movement of the 1700s that urged people to use reason and evidence and to question old authorities
control over what people are allowed to read, write or say
a member of the Society of Jesus, a Catholic order of priests known for running schools

look.title: Two Readings of One Plan
look.text: Reader A: A professor lives where officials decide which books students may read. He forms a quiet club so young people can study freely without losing their future jobs. Reader B: A professor gathers young men in secret, trains them in his ideas and plans to place them in government posts. No one outside can see what they intend.
look.prompt: Both readers describe the same facts. Which words make each reading sound hopeful or dangerous? What further evidence would help you decide between them?

check.q: What did Enlightenment thinkers generally urge people to do?
choices: Use reason and evidence to understand the world
check.why: The reading defines the Enlightenment as a movement that urged people to use reason and evidence.

check.q: What was Weishaupt's connection to the Jesuits?
choices: He was a Jesuit priest who led the order
He was educated at a Jesuit school but was never a Jesuit
He founded the Jesuit order in 1776
He had no contact with Jesuits at all
check.why: The reading says he went to a Jesuit school but was never a Jesuit and opposed their influence.

check.q: Which word means control over what people may read, write or say?
check.why: Censorship is control over what people may read, write or say, which Weishaupt opposed.

lessons.title: Grades and Code Names
lessons.mainIdea: The order ranked members in grades and gave them classical code names; Weishaupt himself was Spartacus.
reading: Inside the order, members were ranked in *grades*. A grade is a level of membership. New members started at the lowest grade. Each one reported to a superior above him, who guided his reading and judged his progress. Only those higher up knew much about the order's leaders and plans.

Members also used *code names*. A code name is a false name used to hide a person's identity. Weishaupt took the name Spartacus. The real Spartacus was an enslaved gladiator who led a great revolt against Rome around 73 BCE. The name hinted that Weishaupt saw himself as a freer of minds.

Code names had a practical use. If a letter was lost or opened, outsiders would not know who wrote it. Later, one member, Baron Adolph Knigge, used the name Philo. Many other members chose names from ancient Greece and Rome. The lists linking code names to real names were among the papers police later found.

Grades, code names and ceremonies were common in secret societies of the time. Freemasons, for example, had grades and private rituals too. In the Illuminati, though, the system also served Weishaupt's control. Members lower down often could not see who was steering the order.

words.d: ranked levels of membership in an order, from beginner to leader
false names used to hide who a person really is
a person of higher rank who guides and judges those below

look.title: A Letter Signed Spartacus
look.text: Picture a folded letter carried from Ingolstadt to Munich. It is signed Spartacus and addressed to Philo. It speaks of new members, books to read and a meeting to plan. A stranger who opens it learns very little. A police officer who also holds a list of code names learns a great deal.
look.prompt: How does a code name protect a member? How does a list of code names, once found, undo that protection?

check.q: What code name did Adam Weishaupt use?
check.why: The reading says Weishaupt took the name Spartacus, after the gladiator who led a revolt against Rome.

check.q: In the order, what was a grade?
choices: A score on a university exam
A level of membership, from beginner upward
A type of code for letters
check.why: A grade is a ranked level of membership; new members started at the lowest one.

check.q: Why did code names matter when the police later seized the papers?
choices: The police found lists linking code names to real names
The code names were written in invisible ink
Members had used their real names all along
The police could not read German
check.why: The reading says lists linking code names to real names were among the papers the police found.

lessons.title: Knigge and the Lodges
lessons.mainIdea: After Baron Adolph Knigge joined in 1780, the order grew by recruiting inside Masonic lodges.
reading: For its first few years the order stayed small. That changed in 1780, when Baron Adolph Knigge joined. Knigge was a writer and a nobleman from northern Germany. He was also an active Freemason. He knew many men who liked ideas, ceremonies and quiet meetings.

*Freemasonry* is a brotherhood that grew out of the stonemasons' guilds. By the 1700s its members met in *lodges*, local branches with their own officers and rituals. Lodges were already networks of educated men across Europe. Knigge saw them as the best place to find new members for the Illuminati.

So the Illuminati began to *recruit* inside Masonic lodges. To recruit means to bring in new members. Some Illuminati joined lodges, then invited chosen brothers into the order. Knigge also helped add higher grades and ceremonies that would appeal to Masons.

This is why the two groups are often mixed up. The Illuminati did not begin inside Freemasonry. Weishaupt founded it separately in 1776. But from about 1780 it grew through Masonic lodges. Most Freemasons of the time never joined it, and many lodges knew nothing about it.

words.d: a brotherhood that grew from stonemasons' guilds and meets in lodges with its own rituals
local branches of the Freemasons, each with its own officers and meetings
to find and bring in new members

look.title: Did the Illuminati Begin Inside Freemasonry?
look.text: Claim: The Illuminati were a secret branch of the Freemasons from the start. Record: Weishaupt founded his order in 1776 as a separate group. After Knigge joined in 1780, members recruited inside Masonic lodges. Many Freemasons never joined the Illuminati or knew of it.
look.prompt: Rewrite the claim so that it matches the record. Which part of the claim is partly true, and which part is false?

check.q: When did Baron Adolph Knigge join the Illuminati?
check.why: The reading says Knigge joined in 1780, and the order grew after that.

check.q: Where did the Illuminati find many new members after 1780?
check.why: Knigge was a Freemason, and the order recruited inside Masonic lodges.

check.q: Which statement best matches the record about the Illuminati and Freemasonry?
choices: The Illuminati were founded as a Masonic lodge
The Freemasons founded the Illuminati in 1776
The order was founded separately, then recruited through lodges
check.why: Weishaupt founded the order on its own in 1776; it later grew by recruiting inside lodges.

lessons.title: How Big Was It?
lessons.mainIdea: No one knows the exact size of the order; historians' estimates range from a few hundred to a little over two thousand members.
reading: How many Illuminati were there? This is a harder question than it looks. The order kept its lists hidden, and not every list survived. Historians build their counts from seized papers, letters and later archive finds. Each source catches only part of the membership.

So historians give an *estimate*, a careful guess based on the evidence. Estimates run from a few hundred members to a little over two thousand. The number depends on who counts as a member. Some men joined and left within a year. Some are known only by a code name.

Famous names make the question harder. Some well-known German writers appear in lists that researchers have put together. How active they were is *disputed*, meaning serious scholars disagree. Appearing on a list does not show that a person attended meetings or shared the order's goals.

Compare this with later rumors that the order held thousands of powerful leaders across Europe. The records show something smaller. It was a network of students, officials, professors and some nobles, mostly in German-speaking lands. It was real, but it was never an army.

words.d: a careful guess about a number, based on the evidence available
argued about by serious scholars who reach different conclusions
a group of people linked by contacts, letters or shared membership

look.title: Counting Hidden Members
look.text: A historian has three sources. A seized list gives 40 real names. A packet of letters mentions 60 code names, and only some of them match the list. A later archive holds essays written by members, some signed and some not. Every source overlaps with the others in some places and misses people in others.
look.prompt: Why would two careful historians using these sources reach different totals? How should a writer report the order's size honestly?

check.q: Why can't historians give one exact membership number?
choices: The order published its full list every year
Lists were hidden, and not all of them survived
Weishaupt counted every member in a census
The order had only three members
check.why: The reading explains that lists were kept hidden and only some survived, so each source catches only part.

check.q: What range do historians' estimates cover?
choices: A few hundred to a little over two thousand
check.why: The reading gives estimates from a few hundred to a little over two thousand members.

check.q: What does it mean that a famous person's role is disputed?
choices: The person certainly led the order
The person wrote the order's rules
check.why: Disputed means serious scholars disagree; appearing on a list does not show how active someone was.

lessons.title: A Split at the Top
lessons.mainIdea: Knigge quarreled with Weishaupt over control of the order and left it on 1 July 1784, then later told his side in print.
reading: As the order grew, its two leaders clashed. Knigge had written ceremonies and brought in many members. He felt he deserved a real say. Weishaupt wanted to keep control of the order's direction. Letters between the men grew angry and bitter. Neither man was willing to give way.

Knigge complained that Weishaupt acted like a *tyrant*, a ruler who holds power alone and harshly. He said Weishaupt demanded obedience from members who had joined to think freely. For a group that praised freedom of thought, this was an awkward charge. Weishaupt, for his part, felt Knigge was changing the order too much.

On 1 July 1784, Knigge formally left the order. His departure was a *schism*, a split inside a group. It came just days after Bavaria's first ban on secret societies, issued on 22 June 1784. The order now faced trouble from outside and inside at the same time.

In 1788 Knigge published his own account of his time in the order. Its short title is Philo's Final Answer, after his code name. A member's own account is a useful *primary source*. It gives an inside view, but it also defends the writer. Historians read it alongside the letters seized by police.

words.d: a ruler who holds power alone and uses it harshly
a split that divides a group into sides
a document or object made by someone who took part in or saw the events

look.title: Reading an Insider's Account
look.text: A former leader writes a book four years after he quit. He explains why he joined, what went wrong and why the founder is to blame. He was there, so he knows details no one else knows. He also wants readers to see him as the reasonable one.
look.prompt: List one reason to trust this account and one reason to be careful with it. What other source could you check it against?

check.q: When did Knigge formally leave the order?
check.why: The reading gives 1 July 1784 as the date Knigge formally left.

check.q: What was the main cause of the split between Knigge and Weishaupt?
choices: A quarrel over control of the order
A disagreement about the American Revolution
A fight over money from a bank
A dispute about which church to attend
check.why: The reading says Knigge wanted a real say while Weishaupt wanted to keep control.

check.q: Why must historians read Knigge's 1788 book with care?
choices: It was written by the police
It gives an inside view but also defends its writer
It is written entirely in code
check.why: A member's own account is a primary source with inside knowledge, but it also defends the writer.

lessons.title: The Edicts of 1784 and 1785
lessons.mainIdea: Between 1784 and 1787 the ruler of Bavaria issued a series of edicts that banned secret societies, first in general and then by name.
reading: Bavaria was ruled by an *elector*, a German prince who had a vote in choosing the Holy Roman Emperor. In the 1780s the Elector was Karl Theodor. Rumors reached his court about a hidden order placing its members in offices. He and his advisers decided to act.

On 22 June 1784, the Elector issued an *edict*, an official order from a ruler that has the force of law. It banned all societies that the state had not approved. It did not name the Illuminati. But every secret group, including the order, now met at its own risk.

On 24 February 1785, members sent the Elector a *petition*, a formal written request to a ruler. They said the order had been misunderstood. It did not help. On 2 March 1785, a second edict named the Freemasons and the Illuminati directly. Another followed on 16 August 1785.

A fourth edict, of 16 August 1787, went further. It made recruiting for the order a crime that could be punished by death. By then the order had already broken apart. The harsh law shows how afraid the government had become of what the order might have been.

words.d: a German prince who had a vote in choosing the Holy Roman Emperor
an official order from a ruler that has the force of law
a formal written request asking a ruler or government to act

look.title: Four Laws in Four Years
look.text: A 1910 Catholic reference work lists four separate Bavarian laws against the Illuminati and other secret groups. It dates them 22 June 1784; 2 March and 16 August 1785; and 16 August 1787. The last one forbade recruiting for the order on pain of death.
look.prompt: Why would a government keep passing new laws against a group that had already been banned? What does the fourth law suggest about officials' fears?

check.q: What did the first edict of 22 June 1784 do?
choices: It banned all societies the state had not approved
It named the Illuminati and ordered Weishaupt's arrest
It made the Illuminati the state church
It closed the University of Ingolstadt
check.why: The reading says the first edict banned all unapproved societies without naming the Illuminati.

check.q: What is a petition?
choices: A law with the force of a ruler behind it
A formal written request to a ruler or government
check.why: A petition is a formal written request; the members sent one to the Elector in February 1785.

check.q: Which edict named the Freemasons and the Illuminati directly?
check.why: The reading says the second edict, of 2 March 1785, named both groups.

lessons.title: Weishaupt Leaves Bavaria
lessons.mainIdea: Weishaupt lost his post in 1785, left Bavaria and lived quietly in Gotha until his death in 1830.
reading: The bans reached Weishaupt quickly. In 1785 he lost his professor's post at Ingolstadt. He left Bavaria to avoid arrest and lived the rest of his life in *exile*. Some of his followers lost their government jobs too. The order he had built over nine years fell apart within months.

Weishaupt found a *patron*, a powerful person who protects or supports someone. Duke Ernst II ruled the small German state of Saxe-Gotha. The duke had an interest in the order himself. He let Weishaupt settle in his city of Gotha, outside Bavarian law.

Weishaupt lived in Gotha for more than forty years. He wrote books defending himself and his ideas. He did not lead a hidden empire. He died there on 18 November 1830, at 82. He had outlived his order by more than forty years, and he never led it again.

This quiet ending matters for later rumors. Many modern stories say the Illuminati went underground and kept growing. Historians find no *documentary evidence*, written records from the time, that the Bavarian order continued after the late 1780s. Groups that use the name today were founded much later.

words.d: a powerful person who protects or supports someone else
living away from one's home country, often to escape punishment
written records made at the time, such as letters, lists and laws

look.title: An Old Man in Gotha
look.text: Picture Gotha around 1820. An old scholar walks through the town to a library. He writes books about philosophy and answers old charges against him. Far away, writers in France, Britain and America are blaming the order he once led for a revolution. They say it is still secretly at work.
look.prompt: What does Weishaupt's quiet life in exile suggest about the claim that his order kept running in secret? Is it proof, or only a clue? Explain.

check.q: Where did Weishaupt settle after leaving Bavaria?
check.why: The reading says Duke Ernst II let Weishaupt settle in his city of Gotha.

check.q: What is a patron?
choices: A powerful person who protects or supports someone
A police officer who searches houses
A member of the lowest grade
check.why: A patron protects or supports someone; Duke Ernst II was Weishaupt's patron.

check.q: What evidence do historians find that the Bavarian order continued after the late 1780s?
choices: Yearly membership lists up to today
Letters Weishaupt wrote as its leader in 1830
No documentary evidence that it continued
Newspaper reports of its meetings in the 1900s
check.why: The reading says historians find no written records from the time showing the order continued.

lessons.title: The Lightning Story
lessons.mainIdea: A famous story says papers found on a man killed by lightning exposed the order, but the official record credits a house search instead.
reading: Many books tell a dramatic story. In July 1785, a priest named Johann Jakob Lanz was traveling near Regensburg. He was a member of the order. Lightning struck and killed him. According to the story, secret papers were found sewn into his clothes, and they exposed the whole order.

The death by lightning is widely reported in older German histories. The papers are another matter. The government's own 1787 books, its *official record*, do not credit Lanz. They say the papers came from a search of Zwack's house in October 1786. The lightning story is a *legend*, a story handed down that may mix fact and invention.

Historians test a story like this by looking for *corroboration*. That means a second, independent source that agrees. The official books were printed by the men who seized the papers. If they had found papers on Lanz, they had every reason to say so. They named a house search instead.

Why did the lightning story spread? It is exciting. It makes it seem as if heaven itself exposed the plot. Good stories travel faster than careful records. A careful reader can enjoy a legend as a legend. The same reader can still say plainly what the evidence shows.

words.d: a story handed down over time that may mix real events with invention
support for a claim from a second, independent source
documents made by a government about its own actions

look.title: Story or Record?
look.text: Version 1: A bolt of lightning kills a messenger, and papers in his coat reveal a secret plot. Version 2: Officers search a former official's house for two days and carry off letters, rule books and lists. The government that ordered the search prints the papers a year later and names the house on the title page.
look.prompt: Which version has corroboration from an official record? Why might Version 1 still be retold more often?

check.q: What part of the Lanz story is not supported by the government's 1787 books?
choices: That papers found on his body exposed the order
That he was a member of the order
That the order existed at all
check.why: The 1787 books credit the house search at Zwack's, not papers found on Lanz.

check.q: What is corroboration?
choices: A story that mixes fact and invention
Support for a claim from a second, independent source
A secret code used in letters
A law issued by a ruler
check.why: Corroboration means a second, independent source agrees with the claim.

check.q: According to the 1787 books, where did the seized papers come from?
choices: A ship in the harbor at Hamburg
A search of Zwack's house in 1786
check.why: The official books name the search of Zwack's house at Landshut in October 1786.

lessons.title: Landshut and Sandersdorf
lessons.mainIdea: Officers seized the order's papers in a search of Zwack's house on 11–12 October 1786 and in a second search at Sandersdorf castle in 1787.
reading: Franz Xaver von Zwack was a former government councillor living in Landshut. He was one of Weishaupt's closest partners in the order. On 11 and 12 October 1786, officers searched his house. They *seized* his papers, which means they took them by legal force.

The haul was large. It included the order's rules, lists linking code names to real names, and letters from Weishaupt. Some papers showed plans to place members in good positions. Others showed members discussing books, morals and how to recruit. For the first time, outsiders could read the order's inner workings.

In 1787 officers searched a second place. It was Sandersdorf castle, home of Baron Thomas von Bassus, another member. More papers were taken there. Together, the two searches gave the government a large *archive*, a collection of records kept together.

A search like this raises hard questions. The members had broken the Elector's law. But the search also exposed private letters to the whole country. Historians are grateful the papers survived. They also remember that the papers reached us through force.

words.d: taken by legal force, as when police take evidence
a collection of records or papers kept together
an official who advises a ruler or serves on a governing council

look.title: The Title Page of 1787
look.text: Some Original Writings of the Order of the Illuminati, which were found at the former government councillor Zwack's during a house search at Landshut on the 11th and 12th of October 1786. Printed by highest command of His Electoral Highness.
look.cite: Einige Originalschriften des Illuminatenordens, Munich, 1787 (title page, translated from German)
look.prompt: List three facts the title page tells you about where the papers came from. Why would a government put these details right on the cover?

check.q: Whose house was searched at Landshut in October 1786?
check.why: The reading and the title page both name Zwack, a former government councillor, at Landshut.

check.q: Where did officers carry out a second search in 1787?
choices: Sandersdorf castle, home of Baron Thomas von Bassus
check.why: The reading says the second search took place at Sandersdorf castle, Baron von Bassus's home.

check.q: What is an archive?
choices: A collection of records kept together
A letter signed with a code name
check.why: An archive is a collection of records kept together, like the papers taken in the two searches.

lessons.title: Printed by Order of the Elector
lessons.mainIdea: In 1787 the Bavarian government printed the seized papers for the public, a new way to turn people against a secret group.
reading: Governments usually hide the evidence they seize. Bavaria did the opposite. In 1787, by order of the Elector, it turned the Landshut papers into a public *publication*, Some Original Writings of the Order of the Illuminati. A second volume, called the Supplement, printed papers from later searches.

The aim was to *discredit* the order, to make people stop trusting or respecting it. Readers could see the members' code names, the founder's plans to place followers in office and quarrels among leaders. Some private letters also embarrassed Weishaupt personally. The government chose what to print and when.

This makes the books a form of *propaganda*. Propaganda is information spread on purpose to shape what people think, often for one side. The papers inside seem to be real. But the way they were chosen, framed and released served the Elector's own goal.

The plan had an effect no one in Munich expected. The printed books spread across Europe. Writers far away read them and imagined an order much bigger than it had been. The government meant to end the Illuminati. Its books helped the Illuminati legend begin.

words.d: to make people stop trusting or respecting someone
information spread on purpose to shape what people think, often for one side
a printed work made available to the public

look.title: From Founding to Printed Papers
look.prompt: How many years passed from the founding to the first ban? From the first ban to the printed papers? What does the timeline say about how long the order really worked?

check.q: Why did the Bavarian government print the seized papers?
choices: To recruit new members for the order
To discredit the order in the public's eyes
To sell them in America for money
check.why: The reading says the aim was to discredit the order, to make people stop trusting it.

check.q: What makes the 1787 books a kind of propaganda?
choices: The papers inside were all forged
They were written by Weishaupt himself
The government chose, framed and released them to serve its goal
check.why: The papers seem real, but the government chose and released them to shape opinion, which is propaganda.

check.q: What unexpected effect did the printed books have?
choices: They helped a legend of a huge order begin across Europe
They made Weishaupt the ruler of Bavaria
They were lost and never read
They proved the order still existed
check.why: The reading says readers far away imagined a much bigger order, so the books helped the legend begin.

lessons.title: What the Papers Actually Show
lessons.mainIdea: The papers show a real, secretive reform club that wanted influence, not a plan it could carry out to take over the world.
reading: What do the printed papers actually show? They show a secret order with ranks, code names and oaths of loyalty. They show a founder who wanted his members to gain influence in schools and government offices. They show plans to spread Enlightenment ideas and reduce church control of learning.

They also show limits. The members argued, quit and struggled to recruit. Much of their writing is about reading lists, moral self-improvement and running their own meetings. A large collection of the order's papers survives today in a Berlin archive. Researchers who study it find many essays that read like homework.

People have drawn different *conclusions* from the same papers. Bavarian officials saw a plot against church and throne. Later admirers saw brave reformers under a harsh government. Both groups read with a *bias*, a leaning that shapes what a person notices and believes.

A fair reading holds both parts. The Illuminati were real, secretive and ambitious. They wanted influence and hid their plans. The papers do not show that they controlled any government, caused a revolution or survived the 1780s. The legend that followed is the subject of the next chapter.

words.d: judgments a person reaches after weighing evidence
a leaning that shapes what a person notices and believes
wanting strongly to gain power, success or influence

look.title: Sort What the Papers Show
look.text: Statement 1: The order used code names and hid its membership. Statement 2: Weishaupt wanted members placed in schools and offices. Statement 3: The order caused the French Revolution of 1789. Statement 4: The order still controls governments today. Statement 5: Members argued and some quit.
look.prompt: Which statements do the 1787 papers support? Which do they not support? Write one sentence explaining the difference.

check.q: Which of these do the seized papers support?
choices: The order ran the French government
Weishaupt wanted members placed in schools and offices
The order had millions of members
check.why: The papers show Weishaupt's plans to gain influence in schools and government offices.

check.q: What is a bias?
choices: A secret code in a letter
A leaning that shapes what a person notices and believes
A level of membership in an order
check.why: A bias is a leaning that shapes what someone notices and believes, as both officials and admirers had.

check.q: What do researchers often find when they read members' surviving essays?
choices: Writing that reads much like homework
check.why: The reading says many surviving essays read like homework on reading, morals and self-improvement.

review.q: Who founded the Order of the Illuminati, and when?
review.why: Adam Weishaupt, a law professor at Ingolstadt, founded the order on 1 May 1776.

review.q: Which aim fits the Enlightenment ideas behind the order?
choices: Reducing church control over what students could learn
review.why: Weishaupt opposed church control of learning and wanted students to read and think freely.

review.q: How did the order grow after 1780?
review.why: After Knigge joined in 1780, the order recruited through Masonic lodges.

review.q: What was Knigge's code name in the order?
review.why: Knigge used the name Philo, and his 1788 book is named after it.

review.q: What did the edict of 2 March 1785 do that the 1784 edict did not?
choices: It named the Freemasons and the Illuminati directly
It allowed the order to meet openly
review.why: The 1784 edict banned unapproved societies in general; the 1785 edict named both groups.

review.q: How do historians treat the story that lightning exposed the order?
choices: As a legend the official record does not support
As a story invented in the 1960s
As the reason Bavaria had an Elector
review.why: The official books credit the house search at Landshut, so the papers-on-Lanz story is treated as legend.

review.q: Which statement about the 1787 printed papers is most accurate?
choices: They were written by the order to recruit members
They were forgeries made by Knigge
They were real papers released by the government to discredit the order
review.why: The Elector ordered the seized papers printed in 1787 to turn the public against the order.

review.q: What do records show about the order after the late 1780s?
choices: It moved to America and grew
No documentary evidence shows it continued
review.why: Historians find no records that the Bavarian order continued; Weishaupt lived quietly in Gotha until 1830.

chapters.title: Barruel, Robison and the Birth of a Legend
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a small Bavarian order that ended in the 1780s become a legend that people still believe today?

story.title: A Warning From the Pulpit
story.kicker: On a fast day in 1798, a famous Boston minister tells his listeners that a secret order is working against America.
paragraphs: It is 9 May 1798, in Boston. President John Adams has asked Americans to spend this day in fasting and prayer. The young United States is in a tense quarrel with France. French ships are seizing American merchant ships at sea. Many people fear war, and some fear enemies at home.

At the New North Church, the Reverend Jedidiah Morse climbs into the pulpit. Many of his listeners know his name. He wrote the geography books their children study. Today his subject is not maps. It is a danger he says has crossed the ocean.

Morse has been reading a new book from Scotland. Its author, a professor named John Robison, claims a secret order called the Illuminati helped cause the French Revolution. Morse warns that the same kind of hidden society may be at work in America. That afternoon he preaches again, across the river in Charlestown.

The sermon is printed and sold. Other ministers take up the warning. Letters about the Illuminati soon reach George Washington at Mount Vernon and, later, Thomas Jefferson. The real order had been broken up in Bavaria more than ten years before. In America, its legend was just getting started.
story.think: Morse spoke on a day when many Americans already feared war. How might fear make a warning about a hidden enemy easier to believe?

lessons.title: The Rosicrucian Manifestos
lessons.mainIdea: Three pamphlets printed in 1614–1616 described a secret Rosicrucian brotherhood that readers tried to join, but no such group ever answered.
reading: In 1614 a short pamphlet appeared in Kassel, a German city. It was called the Fama Fraternitatis, the Fame of the Brotherhood. A second one, the Confessio, followed in Kassel in 1615. Together they are called the Rosicrucian *manifestos*. A manifesto is a public statement of a group's beliefs or aims.

The pamphlets told of a man named Christian Rosenkreutz, or Rose-Cross. He was said to have traveled in the East and gathered hidden wisdom. The Fama says his followers found his tomb 120 years after his death, and his body had not decayed. The brotherhood, it said, would now reform learning and invite worthy men to join.

Across Europe, readers were excited. Some printed open letters asking to join the brotherhood. No documented answer ever came. Historians have found no member lists, meeting records or letters from the brotherhood itself. Most scholars conclude it existed on paper, as an idea.

The manifestos belong to *esoteric* writing, meaning writing about hidden knowledge meant for a small inner circle. They matter here because they set a pattern. A mysterious, invisible brotherhood with secret wisdom became a powerful idea in European imagination, long before the Illuminati.

words.d: public statements of a group's beliefs or aims
about hidden knowledge meant only for a small inner circle
a short printed booklet, often on one subject

look.title: The Rosicrucian Texts in Print
look.cite: Imprints of the Rosicrucian texts; Thomas Vaughan, trans., The Fame and Confession of the Fraternity of R: C:, London, 1652
look.prompt: The three German texts appeared in three years. How long did English readers wait for a translation? How might print help a legend travel?

check.q: Where and when was the Fama Fraternitatis first printed?
check.why: The reading says the Fama appeared in Kassel, a German city, in 1614.

check.q: What happened when readers printed letters asking to join the brotherhood?
choices: They were invited to a meeting in Kassel
They were arrested by the Elector
check.why: The reading says no documented answer came, and no records from the brotherhood exist.

check.q: What does esoteric mean?
choices: About hidden knowledge meant for a small inner circle
Written as a law by a ruler
check.why: Esoteric writing is about hidden knowledge for a small inner circle, like the Rosicrucian manifestos.

lessons.title: A Brotherhood on Paper
lessons.mainIdea: A third Rosicrucian text, the Chymical Wedding, was later claimed by Johann Valentin Andreae, and modern Rosicrucian groups were founded much later.
reading: A third book appeared in Strasbourg in 1616. It was The Chymical Wedding of Christian Rosenkreutz. It tells a seven-day story full of symbols, feasts and tests. It is an *allegory*, a story in which people and events stand for ideas, often religious or moral ones.

The book was *anonymous*, printed with no author's name. Later, a Lutheran pastor named Johann Valentin Andreae said in his autobiography that he wrote it. Scholars debate how seriously he meant it. His role in the two earlier manifestos is disputed. Many historians link all three to a circle of scholars around Tübingen.

Today there are Rosicrucian organizations with real members, meetings and buildings. They were founded in the 1800s and 1900s. Their members' spiritual beliefs deserve respect as beliefs. As a matter of history, though, no documents show a *lineage*, an unbroken line of descent, back to a brotherhood of 1614.

This is a useful lesson for studying any secret society. Old texts can inspire new groups. A new group may honestly feel connected to an old one. A historian still asks a separate question: what records show that the old group actually existed and passed its teachings down?

words.d: a story in which people and events stand for ideas, often religious or moral ones
made or printed without the author's name
an unbroken line of descent from an earlier person or group

look.title: Inspired By or Descended From?
look.text: A club founded in 1915 says its ideas come from the Rosicrucian manifestos of 1614. Its members study the old texts with care. Its leaders say the club carries on the ancient brotherhood. A historian searches archives and finds the 1614 pamphlets, but no letters, lists or meeting records from any brotherhood between 1614 and 1915.
look.prompt: Write two sentences: one that the evidence supports about this club, and one that it does not. How can you say this respectfully?

check.q: Who later said he wrote The Chymical Wedding?
check.why: The reading says the Lutheran pastor Johann Valentin Andreae claimed it in his autobiography.

check.q: What is an allegory?
choices: A story where people and events stand for ideas
A list of a society's members
A public letter asking to join a group
check.why: An allegory is a story in which people and events stand for ideas; The Chymical Wedding is one.

check.q: What do the records show about modern Rosicrucian groups?
choices: They met in secret since 1614 without a break
They were founded in the 1800s and 1900s, with no documented line back to 1614
They were banned in Bavaria in 1785
check.why: The reading says modern groups began in the 1800s and 1900s, and no documents show an unbroken lineage to 1614.

lessons.title: The Golden Dawn, 1888
lessons.mainIdea: The Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn was a real secret order founded in London in 1888, though its founding story rests on disputed documents.
reading: Nearly three centuries later, a real esoteric order appeared in London. In 1888 three men founded the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. They were William Wynn Westcott, a London coroner; William Robert Woodman; and Samuel Liddell MacGregor Mathers. By the end of that year it had three temples, or local groups.

Its members studied old symbols, ceremonies and ideas about hidden knowledge. Its best-known member was the Irish poet W. B. Yeats, who later won the Nobel Prize. His membership is recorded in his own letters and in the order's rolls. Unlike the Rosicrucian brotherhood, the Golden Dawn has members, records and meeting places we can document.

Its founding story is another matter. Westcott said the order came from the *Cipher Manuscripts*, old notes written in a code, and from a German teacher named Anna Sprengel. In 1972 the historian Ellic Howe argued that the Sprengel letters were a *forgery*, a fake made to look real. No independent evidence of Sprengel has been confirmed.

The Golden Dawn split apart after 1900. It shows a pattern seen again and again. A real group can grow from a story about its own origins that cannot be proved. Studying such a group means separating what members did from what they said about their past.

words.d: coded notes that the Golden Dawn's founders said were the source of the order's rituals
a fake document made to look real in order to deceive
in the Golden Dawn, the name for a local group of members

look.title: Two Kinds of Claim
look.text: Claim A: The Golden Dawn was founded in London in 1888 and the poet W. B. Yeats was a member. Claim B: The Golden Dawn received its authority from a German teacher, Anna Sprengel. Claim C: The famous occult writer Aleister Crowley founded the Golden Dawn. Records show Crowley joined in 1898, ten years after the founding.
look.prompt: Label each claim documented, disputed or shown false. What evidence decides each label?

check.q: Where and when was the Golden Dawn founded?
check.why: The reading says three men founded the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn in London in 1888.

check.q: What did the historian Ellic Howe argue in 1972?
choices: That the Sprengel letters were a forgery
That the order began in Bavaria
That the Cipher Manuscripts were written by Weishaupt
check.why: Howe argued the letters from Anna Sprengel were forged; no independent evidence of her has been confirmed.

check.q: Which member of the Golden Dawn is well documented?
check.why: Yeats's membership is recorded in his letters and the order's rolls.

lessons.title: A Shock That Needed an Explanation
lessons.mainIdea: The French Revolution shocked Europe, and some writers explained it as the work of secret societies rather than of many long-building causes.
reading: In 1789 the French Revolution began. Within a few years, France's king was executed. The Catholic Church in France lost its lands and much of its power. Thousands were killed during the Terror of 1793 and 1794. Kings and church leaders across Europe were horrified.

Historians explain the Revolution through many causes. France was deep in debt. Bread prices rose and people went hungry. Many people resented the privileges of nobles and clergy. Enlightenment ideas about rights spread through books and clubs. The most famous club was the *Jacobins*, a political club of radical revolutionaries.

Some writers wanted a simpler answer. They argued that a hidden group had planned it all. This kind of explanation is a *conspiracy theory*, a belief that a secret group secretly causes major events. It can feel satisfying. It gives a clear villain for a confusing and frightening change.

The Illuminati were a tempting villain. Their papers had been printed in 1787, so writers could quote them. But the order had been banned in 1785 and broken up by about 1787. No document shows it directing anything in France. Modern historians reject the idea that it caused the Revolution.

words.d: a political club of radical revolutionaries in France during the 1790s
a belief that a secret group secretly causes major events
a sudden, deep change in a country's government, often by force

look.title: Many Causes or One Plot?
look.text: Explanation 1: France was in debt, bread was expensive, people resented noble privileges and new ideas about rights spread widely. Together these pressures burst into revolution. Explanation 2: A small hidden order planned the whole Revolution from behind the scenes and controlled its leaders.
look.prompt: Which explanation is easier to remember? Which one is better supported by evidence? Why might the easier one spread faster?

check.q: When did the French Revolution begin?
check.why: The reading says the French Revolution began in 1789.

check.q: What is a conspiracy theory?
choices: A belief that a secret group secretly causes major events
A proven history of a government
check.why: The reading defines a conspiracy theory as a belief that a secret group secretly causes major events.

check.q: Why do modern historians reject the claim that the Illuminati caused the Revolution?
choices: The Revolution happened in Germany, not France
Weishaupt was the king of France
The order was broken up by about 1787 and no document shows it directing events
check.why: The order ended years before 1789, and no document shows it directing events in France.

lessons.title: Barruel's Memoirs
lessons.mainIdea: The French priest Augustin Barruel published Memoirs in 1797–98 that blamed the Revolution on a plot of philosophers, Freemasons and Illuminati.
reading: Augustin Barruel was a French Catholic priest, often called the Abbé Barruel. An *abbé* is a French title for a priest or churchman. He fled France during the Revolution and lived for a time in England. There he wrote a long work that shaped how many people saw the Revolution.

His book, in French, was published in 1797 and 1798 in several volumes. An English translation by Robert Clifford came out in London in the same years, as Memoirs, Illustrating the History of Jacobinism. Barruel's *thesis*, his main argument, was that the Revolution grew from a long plot.

In his account, the plotters were anti-church philosophers, then some Freemasons, then the Illuminati. One volume focuses on the Illuminati. It quotes the Bavarian papers of 1787 at length. That is part of why the book seemed convincing. It pointed to real documents.

But quoting a real document is not the same as proving a claim. The papers showed a secret order with plans for influence in Bavaria. They did not show it directing events in France years after it ended. Barruel's book is now studied as the founding text of the modern 'secret group behind the revolution' pattern.

words.d: a French title for a priest or churchman
the main argument that a book or essay sets out to prove
a text turned from one language into another

look.title: A Real Quote, a Big Claim
look.text: A writer quotes a real letter in which a secret-society leader says he wants his members to gain good jobs. The writer then concludes that the society caused a revolution in another country, years after the letter and after the society was banned. The quote is accurate. The conclusion is much larger than the quote.
look.prompt: What does the quote actually prove? What extra evidence would the writer need to support the bigger conclusion?

check.q: What was Barruel's thesis?
choices: That the Revolution grew from hunger and debt alone
That the Revolution grew from a long plot including Freemasons and Illuminati
check.why: Barruel argued the Revolution grew from a long plot of philosophers, some Freemasons and the Illuminati.

check.q: Why did Barruel's book seem convincing to many readers?
choices: It was printed by the Elector of Bavaria
It quoted real Bavarian papers at length
check.why: The reading says Barruel quoted the 1787 Bavarian papers at length, which made the book seem convincing.

check.q: Who translated Barruel's Memoirs into English?
check.why: The reading says Robert Clifford's English translation came out in London in 1797 and 1798.

lessons.title: Robison's Proofs of a Conspiracy
lessons.mainIdea: John Robison, a respected Edinburgh scientist, published Proofs of a Conspiracy in 1797, showing that expertise in one field does not guarantee sound history.
reading: John Robison taught *natural philosophy* at the University of Edinburgh in Scotland. Natural philosophy was the old name for physics and related sciences. He was also secretary of the Royal Society of Edinburgh. Readers trusted him as a serious man of learning.

In 1797 he published a book with a very long title: Proofs of a Conspiracy against all the Religions and Governments of Europe, carried on in the secret meetings of Free Masons, Illuminati, and Reading Societies. It was printed in Edinburgh and London. American editions followed in 1798.

Robison wrote at almost the same time as Barruel, and both used the same Bavarian publications. Barruel said he saw Robison's book late in his own work. Historians note that Robison used the Bavarian papers loosely. He stretched what they showed to fit a large plot across Europe.

Robison's case teaches *source criticism*, the careful testing of a source before trusting it. A great scientist can still be a weak historian. Deep *expertise* in one field does not carry over to every field. Readers must ask what evidence each claim rests on, no matter who makes it.

words.d: the old name for physics and related sciences
the careful testing of a source's evidence before trusting it
deep skill or knowledge in a particular field

look.title: How Fast the Story Traveled
look.cite: Wellcome Collection record for Robison, Proofs of a Conspiracy (1797); Vernon Stauffer, New England and the Bavarian Illuminati (1918)
look.prompt: How many years after the order was banned did Robison's book appear? How many months later did the idea reach a Boston pulpit?

check.q: What did John Robison teach at Edinburgh?
choices: Natural philosophy, the old name for physics
check.why: The reading says Robison taught natural philosophy, the old name for physics and related sciences.

check.q: What did Robison and Barruel have in common?
choices: Both drew on the same Bavarian publications
check.why: The reading says both wrote at almost the same time and used the same Bavarian publications.

check.q: What lesson about expertise does Robison's book teach?
choices: Long titles prove a book is true
Skill in one field does not guarantee sound work in another
check.why: Robison was a respected scientist, but he stretched the evidence as a historian.

lessons.title: Morse and Dwight Sound the Alarm
lessons.mainIdea: In 1798 New England ministers Jedidiah Morse and Timothy Dwight warned Americans that the Illuminati threatened the nation.
reading: In 1798 the United States and France were fighting an undeclared naval war. Historians call it the *Quasi-War*. French ships seized American merchant ships, and many Americans feared a full war. President John Adams called for a national *fast day*, a day of prayer and going without food, on 9 May 1798.

On that day, Jedidiah Morse preached at the New North Church in Boston, then at Charlestown in the afternoon. He was a well-known minister and the author of popular geography books. He was also the father of Samuel F. B. Morse, who later helped invent the telegraph. His *sermon* drew on Robison's book.

Morse warned that an Illuminati-style plot might be spreading in America. The sermon was printed in Boston by Samuel Hall. On 4 July 1798, Timothy Dwight, the president of Yale College, preached at New Haven. His sermon, The Duty of Americans, at the Present Crisis, also named the Illuminati as a danger.

These were not fringe voices. They were leaders of respected churches and colleges. That gave the warning weight. Yet neither man produced evidence of an actual Illuminati lodge in America. The alarm rested on Robison's book and on real fear of France.

words.d: an undeclared naval war between the United States and France, 1798 to 1800
a day set aside for prayer and going without food
a talk on a religious or moral subject given by a preacher

look.title: The Printed Sermon
look.text: The title page describes a sermon delivered at the New North Church in Boston in the morning, and at Charlestown in the afternoon, on 9 May 1798. It notes that the day was the one recommended by John Adams, President of the United States, for solemn humiliation, fasting and prayer.
look.cite: Jedidiah Morse, A Sermon, Delivered at the New North Church in Boston, Boston: Samuel Hall, 1798 (title page)
look.prompt: Why would the printer mention the President on the title page? How might that make readers trust the sermon more?

check.q: Who called for the national fast day of 9 May 1798?
check.why: The reading and the title page both say President John Adams recommended the fast day.

check.q: What was the Quasi-War?
choices: An undeclared naval war between the United States and France
A war between Bavaria and France
A quarrel between two Masonic lodges
check.why: The Quasi-War was an undeclared naval war between the United States and France starting in 1798.

check.q: What evidence did Morse and Dwight give of an actual Illuminati lodge in America?
choices: A police report from New Haven
None; their alarm rested on Robison's book and fear of France
check.why: The reading says neither man produced evidence of an actual Illuminati lodge in America.

lessons.title: Washington Writes Back
lessons.mainIdea: In 1798 George Washington, a Freemason, agreed that Illuminati and Jacobin ideas had reached America but did not believe American lodges were spreading them.
reading: In August 1798 a minister in Frederick, Maryland, named G. W. Snyder wrote to George Washington. Washington had retired to Mount Vernon. Snyder sent him a copy of Robison's book. He warned that the Illuminati might be working inside American Masonic lodges.

Washington was a *Freemason*, a member of the Masonic brotherhood, since 1752. He wrote back on 25 September 1798. He said he had heard much of the Illuminati but had not seen the book before. He added that he rarely went to lodge meetings. He did not believe any American lodge held the Illuminati's principles.

Snyder wrote again. Washington's second reply, of 24 October 1798, drew a careful *distinction*, a clear difference between two things. He said he did not doubt that Illuminati doctrines and Jacobin principles had spread in the United States. But he did not believe the lodges, as bodies, were spreading them, though some members might.

This *correspondence* is a valuable primary source. It shows the scare reached even the most famous man in America. It also shows how a careful reader can be quoted misleadingly. Quote only Washington's first sentence, and he seems to confirm the plot. Read on, and he defends the lodges.

words.d: a member of Freemasonry, a brotherhood that meets in lodges
a clear difference drawn between two things
letters written back and forth between people

look.title: Washington's Second Reply
look.text: Washington writes that he did not mean to doubt that the doctrines of the Illuminati and the principles of Jacobinism had spread in the United States; he says no one is more convinced of it than he is. He then explains that he did not believe the Masonic lodges, as societies, had set out to spread them, though individual members might have.
look.cite: George Washington to G. W. Snyder, 24 October 1798, George Washington Papers, Library of Congress
look.prompt: How would the meaning change if someone quoted only the first sentence? Why should a fair writer always include the second?

check.q: What did Snyder send Washington in 1798?
choices: A copy of Robison's book with a warning
A copy of the Fama Fraternitatis
An invitation to join the Illuminati
check.why: The reading says Snyder sent Robison's book and warned about the Illuminati in American lodges.

check.q: What distinction did Washington draw in his 24 October 1798 letter?
choices: Between ideas spreading in America and lodges as bodies spreading them
check.why: He agreed the ideas had spread but did not believe the lodges, as bodies, were spreading them.

check.q: Why can quoting only Washington's first sentence mislead a reader?
choices: The first sentence is a forgery
The first sentence is about France only
The next sentence defends the lodges and changes the meaning
check.why: The reading says his next sentence defends the lodges, so the first sentence alone seems to confirm the plot.

lessons.title: Politics and the Scare
lessons.mainIdea: The 1798 scare was partly political, and Thomas Jefferson read the same evidence and judged Weishaupt a well-meaning reformer.
reading: In 1798 American politics was bitterly divided. The *Federalists*, the party of President Adams, favored a strong central government and leaned toward Britain. The *Democratic-Republicans*, led by Thomas Jefferson, were friendlier to France. That same year, Congress passed the Alien and Sedition Acts, aimed partly at critics of the government.

Historians, starting with Vernon Stauffer in 1918, argue that the scare was partly *partisan*, driven by party loyalty. Many of the ministers who warned about the Illuminati were Federalists. Linking Jefferson's friends to French radicals and secret plots was a way to attack them.

Jefferson read Barruel's book himself. On 31 January 1800, he wrote to his friend Bishop James Madison of Virginia. Working from Barruel's own quotations, Jefferson judged Weishaupt a sincere lover of humanity. He thought Weishaupt used secrecy because he lived under a harsh church and state that punished free thinkers.

Bishop Madison wrote back that Jefferson's analysis was the most satisfying he had seen. The two readings of Barruel's quotes, by Morse and by Jefferson, show a key idea. The same evidence can lead to opposite conclusions. The reader's fears, hopes and party can shape the result.

words.d: the political party of John Adams, which favored a strong national government
the political party led by Thomas Jefferson, which was friendlier to France
driven by loyalty to a political party

look.title: Jefferson Reads Barruel
look.text: Jefferson tells Bishop Madison that, judging from the passages Barruel quotes, Weishaupt seems to have been an enthusiastic lover of humanity. He suggests Weishaupt kept his work secret because he lived under a harsh church and state that punished people who spread new ideas.
look.cite: Thomas Jefferson to Bishop James Madison, 31 January 1800, Papers of Thomas Jefferson, vol. 31 (Founders Online)
look.prompt: Morse and Jefferson read the same kind of evidence. What did each conclude? What in each man's situation might explain the difference?

check.q: Which party did many of the ministers who warned about the Illuminati support?
check.why: The reading says many of the warning ministers were Federalists, the party of President Adams.

check.q: What did Jefferson conclude about Weishaupt in his 1800 letter?
choices: He was a sincere reformer who used secrecy because of a harsh government
He was secretly ruling the United States
He had caused the French Revolution
check.why: Jefferson judged Weishaupt a well-meaning lover of humanity who hid his work under a harsh church and state.

check.q: What does partisan mean?
choices: Driven by loyalty to a political party
check.why: Partisan means driven by party loyalty, which historians say shaped part of the 1798 scare.

lessons.title: The Eye on the Dollar
lessons.mainIdea: The eye and pyramid on the one-dollar bill come from the Great Seal designs of 1776–1782 and have no documented link to the Illuminati.
reading: Look at the back of a U.S. one-dollar bill. On the left is an unfinished pyramid with an eye in a glowing triangle above it. Many people online call this an Illuminati symbol. The documented history of the design, kept in government records, tells a different story.

In 1776 Congress asked a committee of Benjamin Franklin, John Adams and Thomas Jefferson to design a *Great Seal*, the official stamp of the new nation. Their artist adviser, Pierre Eugène du Simitière, proposed the *Eye of Providence*. It was a common Christian image of God watching over people. In 1782 Congress adopted a pyramid and eye for the back of the seal.

Under the pyramid are the Roman numerals MDCCLXXVI, which mean 1776, the year of independence. The Latin *motto* Novus Ordo Seclorum adapts a line from the Roman poet Virgil. It is usually translated a new order of the ages, meaning a new American era. It does not mean new world order.

The seal's reverse was put on the one-dollar bill in 1935. None of the designers is linked to the Bavarian order. The eye was a familiar symbol long before 1776. A symbol can be shared by many groups without meaning they are connected. Sharing a picture is not the same as sharing a plan.

words.d: the official stamp of the United States, used on important government papers
an eye in a triangle or rays of light, a common Christian image of God watching over people
a short phrase that sums up a belief or aim

look.title: The First Committee's Idea, 1776
look.text: The first Great Seal committee's report of August 1776 described the Eye of Providence in a radiant triangle, its glory spreading over the shield and the figures of the design.
look.cite: Report of the first Great Seal committee, 20 August 1776, printed in Gaillard Hunt, The History of the Seal of the United States (1909)
look.prompt: The eye was proposed in August 1776. The Illuminati were founded in May 1776, in Bavaria, with a handful of students. What does this timing suggest about any link?

check.q: Who proposed the Eye of Providence for the Great Seal in 1776?
check.why: The reading says the artist adviser Pierre Eugène du Simitière proposed the eye to the first committee.

check.q: What does MDCCLXXVI on the pyramid stand for?
choices: The founding date of the Illuminati lodge in America
A secret code for the word Illuminati
1935, the year of the dollar design
check.why: MDCCLXXVI is Roman numerals for 1776, the year of American independence.

check.q: How is Novus Ordo Seclorum usually translated?
choices: A new order of the ages
check.why: The motto adapts Virgil and means a new order of the ages, a new American era.

lessons.title: Satire Taken Seriously
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1960s and 1970s, joke books and satirical novels, one begun in Chicago, spread a playful Illuminati that many readers took seriously.
reading: By the 1900s the Illuminati were a name in old conspiracy books. Then, in the 1960s, the name found new life in jokes. In 1963 Greg Hill and Kerry Thornley produced a playful religious booklet called Principia Discordia. A second edition in 1965 ran to just five copies. It poked fun at secret orders, the Illuminati among them.

The booklet was *satire*, which uses humor and exaggeration to mock ideas or people. The Principia's fans spread made-up Illuminati stories as pranks. Each *hoax* was meant to fool people for fun. A popular tale says its first copies were made on a New Orleans prosecutor's office copier. That detail is disputed, a story the authors liked to tell.

In Chicago in the late 1960s, two magazine editors, Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson, answered readers' letters. Many letters came from people sure that secret groups ran everything. In 1969 the two began a novel that treated every conspiracy theory as true at once. Illuminatus!, a *trilogy* of three books, appeared in 1975.

The novels were satire. Yet many readers took their Illuminati as fact, and ideas from them spread into other books, games and later the internet. In 1964 the historian Richard Hofstadter had already described a style of politics marked by suspicion and fantasies of hidden plots. The Illuminatus! story shows how easily a joke can cross that line.

words.d: writing that uses humor and exaggeration to mock ideas or people
a set of three related books
a trick meant to make people believe something false

look.title: A Legend Reborn in the 1960s
look.cite: Richard Hofstadter, "The Paranoid Style in American Politics," Harper's, November 1964; Shea and Wilson, Illuminatus! (Dell, 1975)
look.prompt: A book of five copies in 1965 became part of a legend millions now know. What changed between 1965 and 1975 that helped the joke spread?

check.q: What is satire?
choices: A trick meant to steal money
Writing that uses humor and exaggeration to mock ideas
A careful history based on archives
check.why: Satire uses humor and exaggeration to mock ideas or people, as Principia Discordia and Illuminatus! did.

check.q: Where did Robert Shea and Robert Anton Wilson begin Illuminatus!?
check.why: The reading says the two editors worked in Chicago and began the novel there in 1969.

check.q: Which detail about Principia Discordia is disputed?
choices: That Greg Hill worked on it
That it poked fun at secret orders
That its first copies were made on a prosecutor's office copier
That a second edition came out in 1965
check.why: The reading calls the copier story disputed, a tale the authors liked to tell.

lessons.title: A Claims Ledger
lessons.mainIdea: A claims ledger sorts statements about the Illuminati into documented, disputed and unsupported, so each claim is judged by its evidence.
reading: Historians often keep a *claims ledger*. A ledger is a record book. A claims ledger lists statements and sorts each by the strength of its evidence. It helps a reader avoid two mistakes: believing everything and believing nothing. Each claim gets judged on its own evidence.

Some Illuminati claims are *documented*, meaning supported by primary evidence. The order was founded in 1776. Bavaria banned it in 1784 and 1785. Its papers were seized and printed in 1787. Morse preached against it in 1798, and Washington and Jefferson wrote about it. Each of these rests on records we can check.

Some claims are disputed, such as how many members the order had or how active famous members were. Others are *unsupported*, meaning no evidence backs them. That the order caused the French Revolution, survives today or includes modern celebrities are all unsupported. The dollar-bill link is shown false by the seal's own history.

One more claim is shown false and also harmful. In the 1900s some writers merged the Illuminati legend with a forged text blaming Jewish people for world events. That forgery spread hatred against real people. A later unit studies how it was exposed. A claims ledger helps readers see such attacks for what they are.

words.d: a record that lists claims and sorts each by the strength of its evidence
supported by primary evidence, such as letters, laws or records
having no evidence to back it up

look.title: Build Your Own Ledger
look.text: 1. Weishaupt founded the Illuminati at Ingolstadt in 1776. 2. The order had more than two thousand members. 3. The Illuminati caused the French Revolution. 4. Washington wrote to G. W. Snyder about the Illuminati in 1798. 5. A famous singer today is secretly an Illuminati leader. 6. The Rosicrucian brotherhood of 1614 was a real organization.
look.prompt: Sort each claim into documented, disputed or unsupported. For one claim in each group, name the evidence or the missing evidence.

check.q: Which claim is documented?
choices: Bavaria's seized Illuminati papers were printed in 1787
The order caused the French Revolution
check.why: The 1787 printed papers exist and can be checked, so this claim is documented.

check.q: What does unsupported mean in a claims ledger?
choices: Having no evidence to back it up
check.why: An unsupported claim has no evidence to back it up.

check.q: Which claim belongs in the disputed column?
choices: The exact number of the order's members
check.why: Historians' estimates of membership differ, so the number is disputed, not settled.

review.q: What did the Rosicrucian manifestos of 1614–1616 describe?
choices: A secret brotherhood that no records show ever existed as a group
The founding of the Golden Dawn
review.why: The manifestos told of a hidden brotherhood, but no member lists or letters from it have ever been found.

review.q: Which two writers of 1797 blamed the French Revolution partly on the Illuminati?
review.why: Barruel's Memoirs and Robison's Proofs of a Conspiracy both appeared in 1797.

review.q: Why was the timing of the Revolution a problem for the Illuminati plot claim?
choices: The Revolution began before the order was founded
The order was founded in France
The order had been broken up by about 1787, before the Revolution began in 1789
review.why: The Bavarian order ended before 1789, and no document shows it directing events in France.

review.q: What was happening between the United States and France when Morse preached in 1798?
choices: An undeclared naval war called the Quasi-War
review.why: The Quasi-War was an undeclared naval conflict, and it made many Americans fearful.

review.q: What did Washington believe about American Masonic lodges in 1798?
choices: That they were run by the Illuminati
That the lodges, as bodies, were not spreading Illuminati ideas
That he led all of them
review.why: Washington said the ideas had spread in America, but he did not believe the lodges as bodies spread them.

review.q: How did Jefferson's reading of Barruel differ from Morse's alarm?
choices: Jefferson saw Weishaupt as a well-meaning reformer, not a plotter
Jefferson thought the Illuminati controlled Congress
Jefferson agreed the Illuminati were in Boston
review.why: In 1800 Jefferson judged Weishaupt a sincere lover of humanity who used secrecy under a harsh government.

review.q: Where does the eye above the pyramid on the dollar bill come from?
review.why: The eye was proposed for the Great Seal in 1776, and the pyramid and eye were adopted in 1782.

review.q: What role did Illuminatus! (1975) play in the legend?
choices: It printed the Bavarian papers for the first time
It was a government report on secret societies
It proved the order still existed
It was satire begun in Chicago that many readers took as fact
review.why: Shea and Wilson wrote the trilogy as satire, but many readers treated its Illuminati as real.
